topic.title: Why the rich borrow money and the poor pay it back

title: Why the rich borrow money and the poor pay it back
description:
Two people borrow on the same day. Why does one loan make her richer and the other make him poorer?
Rohan and Priya take on five kinds of debt: a car loan, a credit card balance, a mortgage, a student loan, and the monthly payment that never ends. Every figure is computed, every assumption said out loud.
The one question that sorts good debt from bad: does it pay you, or do you pay it?

cta: Good debt or bad debt? Tell us which one you have

lines.text: Same day, two loans. Five years on, his car is worth $15,530. Ten years on, her house could be worth $444,073.
I just signed for my dream car. Only $631 a month!
And I signed for a mortgage. Thirty years of payments. Ugh.
Both of them borrowed. But only one of them borrowed the way the rich do.
People think the rich hate debt. We love it. We just never use it the way you do.
So here are five kinds of debt you are likely to carry, the one question that sorts good from bad, and why the most expensive loan is the one that looks cheapest.
Rohan's car costs $35,000. The bank lends him all of it, at 9% a year, for six years.
And the payment is just $631. I can totally afford that.
Just? Rohan, how long is just?
Six years. And then it's all mine. Everyone I know has a car loan anyway.
Everybody can afford the payment, beta. Ask what the car costs you.
Yes. And everyone you know says they are broke.
Rohan isn't foolish. The monthly payment is the only number anyone ever showed him.
The dealer shows him a shiny car and one small monthly number. Here's what that number hides.
72 payments of $631 add up to $45,424. And $10,424 of that is pure interest.
Okay, some interest. But at least I own a really nice car now.
A car starts losing value the day it leaves the lot. Assume it loses fifteen percent a year. After five years, his is worth $15,530.
So after five years, he has paid a lot, and he owns a car worth less than half its price. Here is the damage.
He borrowed $35,000. The car has already lost $19,470 of it.
So the loan bought something that shrinks. And he pays interest the whole time it shrinks.
Wait. I'm paying the bank to watch my car get cheaper?
Exactly. That is debt working against you. Every month, a little more of your pay walks out the door.
But I need a car to get to work.
Sure. But needing a car and needing that car are two very different things.
That's the first difference. The poor borrow for things that lose value. The rich borrow for things that gain it.
Rich people buy cars too. Usually with money they've already made, and often a cheaper car than they could afford.
And a car loan, at least, ends. The next debt can follow you for 15 years.
It started with one dinner he couldn't quite afford. Then a jacket on sale. Then a trip with friends.
Rohan's card has a balance of $5,000. The interest rate is 22.8% a year.
No problem. The app says I only have to pay $150 this month.
But I pay every single month. I'm never late!
Paying on time keeps the late fees away. It doesn't touch the interest.
The minimum is a small slice of the balance. At first, most of it goes straight to interest.
A low minimum feels kind. But the longer you take to pay, the more interest the bank earns.
Picture a bucket with a hole. He pours in $150 a month, and interest leaks most of it straight back out.
After a whole year of payments, he still owes $4,348.
I have seen this film before. It runs for 15 years.
Paying only the minimum, his balance crawls toward zero for 15 years.
15 years? I'll have kids in school by then!
The interest alone adds up to $6,746. More than the whole balance he borrowed.
So the card bought dinners and a jacket. And he's still paying for them years later.
The jacket is already out of fashion!
Rich people use cards too. They pay the full statement every month, and the bank earns nothing from them in interest.
So that's two debts. A car that shrinks and a card that never ends. Next, the debt the rich actually like.
Priya buys a home for $300,000. She puts some savings down, and borrows $240,000.
Thirty years at 6.5%. That's $1,517 every month. A lot of payments.
Why didn't she just keep renting? No mortgage, no stress.
Rent buys me a place to live this month. A mortgage payment also buys me a little more of the house.
Here's the honest number first. Over thirty years, the bank collects $306,107 in interest.
That's way more interest than my car! So she's worse off than me?
Not so fast. Look at what her loan bought.
Assume homes in her town grow 4% a year. That's an assumption, not a promise.
Ten years later, her house could be worth $444,073.
Could be? So it might not be?
Could be. That's the honest word. Nobody knows what house prices will do next.
That's $144,073 more than the price. And that growth is mine, not the bank's.
The bank gets its interest. She gets the growth on the whole house, not just on the part she paid.
That's called leverage. Borrow most of the price, and the whole thing grows for you.
Notice what each of them signed for. Rohan, a car that loses value every year. Priya, a house that can gain value.
Here's the second difference. The rich borrow at low rates. The poor borrow at high ones.
And she pays 6.5%, while his card charges 22.8%. Cheap money is the rich person's favourite tool.
Banks charge less when a loan is backed by something valuable, like a house.
And my card is backed by... a jacket.
The catch: a house also costs taxes, insurance and repairs. And prices can fall. In some years, they did.
So a house can make you richer. But it's not free money.
Right. The question is never the monthly payment. It's what the loan buys.
His car payment buys a ride. My mortgage payment buys a roof, and a little more of the house every month.
And the next loan doesn't buy a thing you can touch at all. It buys a skill.
Priya's cousin borrows $30,000 for a degree, at 6.5%, over ten years.
That's $341 a month, and $10,877 in interest.
About the same interest as Rohan's car loan. But a very different bet.
So it's just another loan, like my car.
It depends on one thing. What does the course do to the salary?
If the degree lifts her pay by more than $341 a month, the loan pays for itself, and then some.
And if it doesn't, it's a car loan with a diploma.
A car loan with a diploma. Okay, I'm stealing that one.
Before I signed anything, I asked what people with that degree actually earn.
Rohan took an online course once too. He never asked what it would pay him back.
If a course can't tell you what its students go on to earn, that's your answer.
What course was it, Rohan?
How to get rich from home. It had really good reviews.
The skill loan is the one rich people take most happily: a loan on themselves. But only when the numbers say it pays.
A skill can't be repossessed, and it can't lose value sitting in a parking lot.
So before the next course, I check what it pays first. Got it.
Good. That one habit puts you ahead before you borrow a cent.
So that's four debts. Two bought things that shrink. Two bought things that can grow.
Next, the one question that sorts every loan you will ever take.
Before any loan, I ask one thing. Does it pay me, or do I pay it?
So compare two numbers. What the debt costs a year, and what the money could earn a year.
Rohan's card costs 22.8% a year. Assume a broad stock market fund returns 8% a year over the long run.
Paying off that card is like earning 22.8% on your money. No fund promises you that.
So clearing my card is the best deal I've got?
That's why rich people rarely carry a card balance. That debt only ever pays the bank.
Her mortgage costs 6.5%. Her home, if it grows 4% a year, gives her growth on the whole price.
On paper, the interest costs her a bit more than the growth. But she also gets a place to live, and a fixed payment that does not rise with rent.
Now run every loan through that one question.
Card: I pay it. Car: I pay it. Her house: it can pay her. The degree: it depends.
If the borrowed money earns more than its rate, the debt works for you. If not, you work for the debt.
And Rohan's car loan? It costs 9% a year, for a thing that loses value every year. It fails the question twice.
So here's most of the rule. Cheap debt, for things that can grow. No debt, for things that shrink.
So what should I do with my card right now?
We don't tell anyone what to do. But you can run the question yourself, on every loan you have.
But there's one debt that looks cheaper than all of them. And many people carry it their whole lives.
Six years later, Rohan finally pays off the car. So what does he do next?
New car! Same payment, new smell.
Many people always have a car payment. One loan ends, and the next one starts.
So what if the same $631 went into investments instead, every month?
Investments? Isn't that only for people who are already rich?
It's how a lot of people become rich. Slowly, with ordinary amounts like this one.
At an assumed 8% a year, six years of that payment grows to $58,455.
And that is from just one car.
That's more than the whole car cost me!
Now keep it going for thirty years, the way many people keep a car payment.
Okay. How much are we talking?
Thirty years of that payment, invested, becomes $946,686.
Not because the payment was big. Because it never stopped, and it had thirty years to grow.
He would have put in $227,160. The other $719,526 is growth.
And that's with no stock tips and no luck. Just a payment that stayed home every month.
That is the payment people call cheap.
All of that, parked in my driveway.
To be fair, you still need a car. But a cheaper one, kept longer, frees up most of that payment.
And markets don't go up in a straight line. 8% is an assumption, and some years will be down.
At your age, I rode a scooter, not a new car. And every month, I paid myself the car payment instead.
Wait. Is that why you live in a penthouse?
That, and a lot of patience.
So, five debts. A car and a card that shrink. A house and a skill that can grow. And a payment that never ends.
So here is how the rich borrow. Cheap money, for things that pay them back.
Okay. Next car: a cheaper one, and I keep it longer.
And the poor borrow expensive money for things that don't. Does your loan pay you, or do you pay it?
Our maths is simplified: before tax, fees and upkeep, with assumed growth rates. Good debt or bad debt? Tell us which one you have.
